app.subtitle: Iraq · Ministry of Health 2023 screening guidelines, with WHO, IARC, NHS and CDC evidence
form.intro: Answer a few questions. The tool applies the Ministry of Health 2023 screening guidelines to your answers and shows which screening tests are recommended for you.
results.intlBased: International evidence (not covered by the Ministry of Health guideline)
results.footer: Take this plan to your family doctor or the nearest primary health care centre.
about.body: This tool helps people in Iraq understand which cancer screening tests are recommended for them. Until the Iraqi national guideline is added, it applies the rules of the Ministry of Health Cancer Screening Clinical Practice Guidelines (2023, V01) for breast, cervical, colorectal, lung and prostate cancer. Where the guideline is silent (for example on upper age limits), it says so and uses WHO, IARC, NHS, USPSTF and CDC evidence, which is also shown for comparison.
about.translation: The Sorani, Badini and Arabic texts were machine-drafted and must be reviewed by native-speaking clinicians before public use.
share.text: Find out which cancer screening tests are right for you, based on the Ministry of Health guidelines.
tr.review: The Sorani, Badini and Arabic texts were drafted by machine. Please correct anything that is wrong or unclear and send the file to the developers.
breast.high.groups: Your answers place you in Ministry of Health high-risk group(s): {groups}.
breast.high.genetic: Ask for referral to a genetic counsellor or a doctor experienced in cancer genetics (Ministry of Health group C).
breast.high.mri35to40: Breast MRI or mammogram every year (Ministry of Health guideline: ages 35 to 40).
breast.high.gap41to44: The Ministry of Health guideline specifies yearly MRI/mammogram at 35 to 40 and yearly mammogram from 45; ages 41 to 44 are not specified. International high-risk guidance (NCCN) continues yearly imaging, so discuss continuing yearly imaging with your doctor.
breast.high.annualMammo: Mammogram every year (Ministry of Health guideline: ages 45 to 69).
breast.avg.startAt45: For women at average risk, the Ministry of Health guideline starts mammography screening at age 45.
breast.avg.biennial: Screening mammogram (2 views) every two years from age 45 to 69 (Ministry of Health 2023).
breast.over69: The Ministry of Health programme covers ages 45 to 69. Whether to continue depends on your health; some international programmes continue to 74.
lung.excludedDetail: The Ministry of Health guideline excludes people whose health would not allow curative treatment, because they would not benefit from early detection.
lung.criteriaSmoking: Age 55 to 70 with more than 30 pack-years, still smoking or quit within the last 10 years (Ministry of Health high-risk criteria).
lung.criteriaOccupational: Occupational exposure to lung carcinogens (Ministry of Health guideline: one additional criterion is enough for LDCT referral).
lung.criteriaCopd: COPD or pulmonary tuberculosis (Ministry of Health guideline: one additional criterion is enough for LDCT referral).
lung.over70: The Ministry of Health programme covers ages 55 to 70. USPSTF continues yearly LDCT to age 80 for people who smoked 20 or more pack-years and quit within 15 years.
lung.under55: Under the Ministry of Health guideline lung screening starts at 55. (USPSTF starts at 50 with 20 or more pack-years.)
lung.notEligible: You do not meet the Ministry of Health high-risk criteria for lung screening.
prostate.lifeExpectancyDetail: Ministry of Health guideline: never screen men with a life expectancy below 10 years; they are unlikely to benefit because prostate cancer often grows slowly.
prostate.riskStart45: Ministry of Health guideline: well-informed men with risk factors may start PSA screening at 45.
prostate.noRiskUnder55: Ministry of Health guideline: screening is not recommended under 55 without risk factors (low incidence, little evidence of benefit, risk of false positives).
prostate.age55to72: Ministry of Health guideline: men aged 55 to 72 may be screened after being informed about the limited benefits and substantial risks.
prostate.over72: Ministry of Health guideline: do not screen after 72 unless life expectancy is more than 10 years. Overall health matters more than age alone.
prostate.psa.over10: PSA above 10: the Ministry of Health guideline advises transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) and prostate biopsy.
prostate.psa.4to10Abnormal: PSA 4 to 10 with an abnormal rectal exam: the Ministry of Health guideline advises TRUS and prostate biopsy.
prostate.psa.under4Abnormal: PSA below 4 but abnormal rectal exam: the Ministry of Health guideline advises TRUS and prostate biopsy.
prostate.psa.2_5to4: PSA 2.5 to 4 with no abnormal exam: retest every year (follow up in 1 to 2 years per the Ministry of Health guideline).
lung.criteriaTammemagi: Tammemagi calculator 6-year risk above 2% (Ministry of Health high-risk criterion).
cervical.notActive: Ministry of Health guideline: cervical screening should begin within 3 years after a woman becomes sexually active. You do not need it yet.
cervical.under30: The Ministry of Health programme invites married women from age 30. In the private sector screening can start at 25, and it should begin within 3 years after starting sexual activity (Ministry of Health guideline). Ask your doctor.
cervical.methods: Ministry of Health guideline: HPV DNA test every 5 to 10 years, or Pap smear (cytology) every 3 years until 49. Co-testing (both) is also accepted.
cervical.methods50: Ministry of Health guideline: HPV DNA test every 5 to 10 years, or Pap smear every 5 years from 50 to 69.
cervical.unscheduled: The Ministry of Health guideline also advises an extra test when starting birth-control pills, having an IUD fitted, starting HRT, being diagnosed with genital warts or a pelvic infection, or before gynaecological surgery.
cervical.immuno: The Ministry of Health guideline has no separate schedule for weakened immunity. WHO advises HPV testing every 3 to 5 years from age 25 for women living with HIV. Ask your doctor.
cervical.over69: The Ministry of Health schedule ends at 69. Whether to continue depends on your previous results; ask your doctor.
cervical.over69Stop: The Ministry of Health schedule ends at 69. With normal results over the last 10 years, screening can usually stop (WHO and USPSTF agree).
crc.polyps: After polyps are removed, the next colonoscopy is due in 1 to 10 years depending on their size, number and type (Ministry of Health guideline). Surveillance stops if life expectancy is under 10 years.
crc.moderate: Moderate risk (Ministry of Health guideline): one first-degree relative diagnosed at 60 or older, or two second-degree relatives. Colonoscopy from age 40, repeated every 10 years.
crc.high: High risk (Ministry of Health guideline): two or more first-degree relatives, or one diagnosed before 60. Colonoscopy from age {start} (age 40, or 10 years before the youngest relative’s diagnosis if earlier), repeated every 5 years.
crc.notYetFamily: With your family history, colonoscopy starts at age {start} (Ministry of Health guideline).
crc.start: Ministry of Health guideline: screening for people at average risk starts at 45.
crc.options: Ministry of Health guideline: colonoscopy (the gold standard) every 10 years from 45 to 75. If you do not want colonoscopy, a stool test (FIT) every year instead; a positive FIT needs a colonoscopy.
crc.age76to85: Ministry of Health guideline: routine screening is not recommended at 76 to 85 unless you are healthy and have never been screened. Decide with your doctor based on life expectancy.
ai.intro: Ask questions about screening in your own language. The assistant is grounded in the Ministry of Health 2023 guideline and WHO, IARC, NHS and CDC evidence.
chart.packThreshold: Ministry of Health lung screening needs more than 30
